$comment: Per-route performance budgets. The single authority for the build gate and,
when it lands, the Lighthouse CI assertion config -- section 22 requires the
budget to live in configuration, and two configuration files would be the
two-sources defect wearing another costume.
Section 22: 'every route in the CI budget file carries a numeric threshold',
with 180KB critical-path JS and LCP under 2.5s on throttled 4G as the default
for any route that has not ratified its own. So `status` records PROVENANCE --
where a number came from -- and never replaces the number. A route whose
status is `inherited` still states its threshold explicitly, because a reader
checking compliance must not have to resolve a default in their head.
180KB is read as 180000 bytes, not 184320. The conservative reading.
status:
inherited   takes the default; the number is copied here deliberately
explicit    ratified its own ceiling; `reason` is mandatory
exempt      not gated; `reason` is mandatory
Raising a threshold is its own commit, carrying the measured number and the
reason. Never in the commit that made it red.
A stable proxy for transfer size, not a prediction of it: a real CDN may
use a different level or Brotli and will land lower. Validated against
the running production server at 0.25% difference.
Excludes the legacy `noModule` polyfill bundle, which no browser that
understands ES modules ever requests. Including it cost 39520 B and put
the employee route over the default on the first measurement -- an
exemption earned by bytes nobody downloads.
A growth tripwire on the AUTHORED stylesheets, and deliberately not a
claim about transfer size. Nothing here measures shipped CSS: the route
metric above is JavaScript only, so CSS growth was unbudgeted by
construction rather than by oversight. Stating that plainly beats a
number that implies coverage it does not have.
COMMENTS ARE STRIPPED BEFORE MEASURING. They are 44% of ui.css raw --
4770 B gzipped whole against 1570 B as declarations -- so gating the
file would spend two thirds of the budget on prose, in a repository
whose conventions ask for exactly that prose. A budget that taxes
documentation is one people route around, which is the failure
CLAUDE.md describes as a rule followed past the reason for it.
Minification removes them from what ships anyway.
wants: it should fire on alarming growth, not on ordinary work. It is
not yet a hard budget, because normal movement is not yet known -- one
more wave of real numbers is what promotes it.
THE PROMOTION THIS NOTE ASKED FOR HAS HAPPENED. It used to end "normal
movement is not yet known -- one more wave of real numbers is what promotes
it". Six foundations have since landed -- typography, elevation, spacing and
density, shape, motion and state, layout -- and the movement is now known:
roughly 10.7 gzipped bytes per role, growing only when a role is minted.
So the rule is no longer "sit near half the default". It is: A BUDGET CLEARS
THE PROJECTED CEILING BY ABOUT 30%. The projection is the roles already
decided and not yet built, which this repository writes down rather than
leaves implied -- so the number is derivable rather than a matter of taste,
and the next raise has to show its arithmetic the same way.

largestContentfulPaintMs.tool: not yet implemented -- Lighthouse CI, 5 runs, median
$comment: Section 22's 'throttled 4G' is the condition. Recorded here so the
threshold is not mistaken for one measured on an unthrottled desktop.
Lighthouse cannot measure INP -- it is a navigation test with no real
interaction -- so TBT stands in there and interaction latency is
measured in Playwright instead.
591 B when the superseding system's vocabulary landed: 63 roles, one
@theme inline declaration each. Generated from the same token file as
tokens.css beside it, so it grows in lockstep with the vocabulary and
never on its own.

packages/design/generated/tokens.css.reason: The one file whose size is a direct function of the vocabulary: 224 roles at 10.7 gzipped bytes each, emitted across a base block and three modes. It clears the projected ceiling of ~2784 B -- the component tier, the recorded adaptive pane roles and the first list/detail screens -- by about 30%, which is the rule the metric note now states. Higher than the 2400 default because four other assets share that default and none of them grows with the token file.
$comment: RAISED 2400 -> 3600 at 2389 B, with the count and the arithmetic, which is
what a tripwire is for.
MEASURED: 2389 B for 283 declarations across base and three mode blocks --
224 distinct roles at 10.7 B each. The file was at 100% of its budget with
11 B spare, which is not headroom, it is a wall.
PROJECTED CEILING ~2784 B. What is known to be still coming:
component tier        12 roles   the ceiling another guard already holds
adaptive pane roles  ~15 roles   recorded in POLICY, deliberately not built
list/detail screens  ~10 roles   estimate
3600 clears that by 816 B -- about 76 roles beyond anything planned -- so it
fires on a vocabulary growing half again, and not on ordinary work.
WHY NOT A MARKET NUMBER. The 2025 Web Almanac puts median CSS transfer size
at 82 KB across 17.2M sites. That figure is about SHIPPED CSS and this metric
measures authored declarations with comments stripped -- importing it would
set a threshold 20x above anything this file could reach, which is the shape
ADR-024 calls installed, configured, green and blind. The shipped budget is a
different instrument and does not exist yet; see the metric note.

apps/web/app/globals.css.reason: An entry point and two custom utilities, not a stylesheet. Tighter than the 2400 B default because every design value is supposed to arrive through the generated bridge, and a budget it cannot grow into is what keeps that true.
$comment: 238 B when it landed: four at-rules and the two width utilities Tailwind
has no namespace for. Unlike globals.css this file IS read by the CSS
guards -- it sits under packages/**, so a literal or a primitive
reference is refused. The budget is the second line of defence, against
growth the guards permit but nobody intended.
RAISED 500 -> 700 at 540 B, deliberately and with the count, which is what
a tripwire is for. What crossed it:
two stacking utilities        z-index has no Tailwind namespace
h-control, size-icon          the density axis had nothing to move
four duration utilities       duration-<n> is computed, not a theme key
animate-shimmer + keyframes   replaces Tailwind animate-pulse so the loop
duration is a token the policy governs
prefers-reduced-motion        RESTORED. The system this replaces had it and
the cutover dropped it; the only trace left was
a compiled artefact under .next.
Every one of those is a value Tailwind gives no namespace to, which is the
category this file exists for. It is not styling that leaked in -- the CSS
guards still refuse a literal here, and they fired twice during this change.
RAISED 700 -> 900 at 539 B (77%), by the same rule as tokens.css: clear the
projected ceiling by about 30%. Since the last raise this file gained the
reduced-motion block, four duration utilities and the shimmer keyframes, and
the remaining known work is small -- a couple of utilities for properties
Tailwind has no namespace for.

apps/web/app/globals.css.reason: Tighter than the 2400 B default on purpose: this is an entry point, not a stylesheet, and it is the one stylesheet no CSS guard reads.
$comment: 146 B when the Tailwind pipeline landed, and it should stay near that.
Four at-rules and no declarations of its own by design -- every design
value reaches Tailwind through the generated bridge instead.
tokens-are-the-authority and stylesheet-names-roles-not-primitives are
both scoped to packages/design/**.css, so a literal written here would be
caught by nothing. A budget it cannot grow into is the only thing
standing between this file and becoming a second home for design values.
Framework routes, carrying almost no application code. They are here as
the cheapest early warning that exists: when the Next or React baseline
grows, these move first and for a reason that is not our doing.
